title: Regions & Geography
summary: How US geography shapes demand: the four Census regions and the Sun Belt shift, a suburban and car-based way of life, climate seasonality, and state-by-state rules. Explains why density, not just income, decides whether delivery and small-format retail work.

blocks.note: The South grew ~6% from 2020 to 2025 vs ~3% nationally (Census Vintage 2025).

blocks.title: The Sun Belt shift
blocks.body: The 'Sun Belt' is the band of southern and southwestern states from the Carolinas and Florida through Texas to Arizona. Lower taxes, cheaper housing and remote work have pulled people and companies there for decades, accelerated after 2020. Growth concentrates in outer suburbs of metros like Dallas, Houston, Atlanta and Phoenix. For retailers and restaurants, this is where new stores open; the Northeast and Midwest are more about optimizing existing footprints.

blocks.title: Urban, suburban, rural
items: ~80% of Americans live in Census-defined urban areas (2020), but most of that is low-density suburb, not city core.
In a housing survey, ~52% of households described their neighborhood as suburban, ~27% urban, ~21% rural (AHS 2017).
Urbanization ranges from ~89% in the West to ~74% in the Midwest (2020 Census).
Rural America is older and lower-income on average, with longer drives to stores and fewer delivery options.

blocks.title: Car dependence and commuting
items: ~69% of workers drove alone to work in 2024; only ~4% used public transit; ~13% worked from home (ACS).
Only ~8% of households have no vehicle; ~59% have two or more (2023, BTS).
Implication: big-box stores with parking, drive-thrus, weekly stock-up trips and curbside pickup are the default retail model.
Transit-dependent markets (NYC, parts of Chicago, SF, Boston, DC) behave very differently; don't generalize from them.

blocks.title: Climate effects on demand
items: Seasonality is strong: winter coats, snow tires and heating in the North; summer AC, pools and beverages peak nationwide.
The 'back-to-school' (Jul-Sep) and holiday season (Nov-Dec) calendars matter more than weather for most retailers.
Hurricanes (Gulf/Atlantic, Jun-Nov) and wildfires (West) drive stock-up spikes, insurance costs and supply disruptions.
A warm winter can hurt apparel and utilities in one region while helping restaurants and home improvement.

blocks.title: State differences that change the case
items: Nine states have no broad wage income tax, including Texas, Florida, Washington, Nevada and Tennessee.
Five states have no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon; elsewhere state plus local rates vary widely.
Prices are usually shown before sales tax, which is added at checkout and differs by city.
California often sets de facto national rules: vehicle emissions, product labeling (Prop 65), privacy (CCPA), and gig-worker law.
Alcohol, cannabis, pharmacy and insurance are regulated state by state, so a national rollout can mean 50 rulebooks.

blocks.title: Why density drives delivery and retail economics
blocks.body: Delivery cost per order falls when many orders sit close together: more drops per hour, shorter rides, smaller dark stores turning inventory fast. The US averages ~37 people per km² vs ~484 in India (World Bank, 2023), and most Americans live in spread-out suburbs. So US delivery leans on larger baskets, scheduled slots, fees and subscriptions, while ultra-fast delivery works mainly in dense cores like Manhattan.

blocks.title: Ask 'where' before 'how much'
blocks.body: In delivery, retail-expansion or real-estate cases, ask which metros and what density. A dark-store model that pencils out in Manhattan may lose money in suburban Phoenix. Splitting the market into dense urban cores vs suburbs vs rural often unlocks the answer.

in_a_case: Quick-commerce expansion in the US: segment cities by density first; only a handful of urban cores support sub-30-minute delivery profitably.
Store-network growth for a restaurant chain: favor fast-growing Sun Belt suburbs with drive-thru sites over saturated Northeast metros.
A national retailer's Q3 miss: check regional weather (warm fall, hurricane) before blaming merchandising.
Pricing case: remember sales tax is added at checkout and varies by state and city; 'shelf price' is pre-tax.
Launching a regulated product: plan state-by-state; California rules often become the national standard.

flashcards.back: Northeast, Midwest, South, West. The South is largest and fastest-growing.
